title: Two hours in nature
hookLine: people spending about 120 minutes a week in nature reported better health

cards: A survey question, plain as a form at the doctor's office: last week, how much time did you spend out in nature? Parks, woods, a beach, a path along a canal.
Researchers in England asked about twenty thousand people questions like that, then lined the answers up against how they rated their own health and well-being. A line showed up. Not at five minutes.
Not at a whole weekend away. Somewhere around two hours a week. The question is how much weight that line can carry.

teach.b: First, the finding. The study, by Mathew White and colleagues, appeared in the journal Scientific Reports.
People who'd spent at least about 120 minutes in nature in the past week were more likely to report good health and high well-being than people who'd spent none. Below that, no clear link.
Above it, the benefit leveled off rather than climbing forever. Second, the shape.

teach.h: ONE WALK OR SEVERAL, BOTH COUNT.
teach.b: It didn't seem to matter whether the two hours came as one long walk or several short ones, and the pattern held for older adults and for people living with long-term health conditions. Third, the limits.
This was a snapshot survey: people reported their own time outdoors and their own health. So it can't say which way the arrow points; healthier people may simply get outside more.
Two hours is a pattern in the data and a sensible target, not a proven dose. Fourth, an older voice.

teach.h: I CANNOT PRESERVE MY HEALTH AND SPIRITS.
teach.b: Henry David Thoreau, in his essay Walking, set his own bar far higher: "I think that I cannot preserve my health and spirits, unless I spend four hours a day at least" out in the woods and fields.
He wasn't measuring anyone; he was describing his own life. The survey and the essay meet in a modest place: time outside can go on the calendar, like anything else that matters.

how: People who follow this research often treat about two hours a week outdoors as a rough weekly target, split however their week allows, while remembering it comes from a survey, not a trial.

games.q: what does “two hours in nature” mean?
o: about 120 minutes outside a week, linked with better health
a proven daily dose that cures stress and illness
the minimum time a hike needs to do any good

games.q: two hours in nature: tap the pairs.
p: four hours a day, in Walking

s: the survey found you need a whole weekend away to see a difference
the line showed up around two hours a week, and short visits added up just as well as one long one.
it didn't seem to matter whether the two hours came in one visit or several
one long walk or several short ones: the pattern looked the same.
the study proved that time in nature causes better health
it was a snapshot survey of what people reported. healthier people may simply get outside more.

games.q: you can't fit one long two-hour walk into your week. going by the survey, what's the sensible move?
o: give up until you have a free weekend.
split it into shorter visits across the week.
stay out for ten hours once to make up for it.
games.why: in the survey it didn't seem to matter whether the time came in one visit or several. and above about two hours, the benefit leveled off.

practice: Walk through the coming week in your mind and find the nearest green or open place: a park, a tree-lined street, a riverbank, a backyard, a rooftop with sky.
Then find when you could go, one long stretch or twenty minutes on several days. Settle on one real place and one real time, and picture yourself already there.

wordCard.voice: Two hours in nature. About 120 minutes a week, the line a large survey linked with better reported health. A pattern, not a prescription. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: two hours a week. One long walk or several short ones, both count. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: White, M. P., et al., "Spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature is associated with good health and wellbeing," Scientific Reports (2019)

sources.q: I think that I cannot preserve my health and spirits, unless I spend four hours a day at least
